paragraphs.text: Listen for the chance of a lifetime.
Jenkins is telling David about a great opportunity, but should David invest in it?
Listen to their conversation and answer the comprehension questions.
No way, uh-uh, not my hard earned dollars.
It's the chance of a lifetime, Dave.
Lighten up, man.
Jenkins, you're nuts if you think I'm going to invest $4,000 into a stock that I know nothing
about.
We've known each other since the second grade.
You can trust me, man.
Would I lead you astray?
Yes, you would.
Remember the time you talked me into buying that 1967 convertible Volkswagen?
The chance of a lifetime, you told me.
That clunker cost me more repairs than I can't remember.
Okay, okay.
So I was wrong about that.
No one's perfect, but this is different, Dave.
Ocean Tech is going to take the world by surprise.
Do you know that Ocean Tech is developing a new sonar technology that the Navy is interested
in buying?
Dave, if we invest now we'll be millionaires.
Ocean Tech stocks are dirt cheap right now.
I've never even heard of Ocean Tech Jenkins, and I work for the Department of Defense.
If a deal involving the Navy was in the works, I would be aware of it.
Dude, I'm your pal.
I'm offering you a chance of a lifetime, and all you do is give me the third degree.
Jenkins, I have $8,000 in savings.
Mandy and I are getting married in four months.
I still have to save up another $7,000 to make the down payment for the house I want to
buy Mandy.
I ain't about to gamble with my money.
But just think, if you buy $4,000 worth of Ocean Tech stocks at $20 a stock, and then Ocean
Tech sells the stocks for $80, you'll make a fortune.
Nothing in life is that easy, Jenkins.
Sounds to me like this Ocean Tech company is a scam.
And man, do you fall for scams?
Let me guess, some smooth talking guy in a fancy suit, driving a fancy car came into your
coffee shop and told you about Ocean Tech.
Maybe even showed you some papers, charts, graphs?
Oh, well, okay.
Sure, Mr. Rogers showed me some papers.
But the papers he showed me were well researched.
And he used a lot of business lingo, right?
He spoke with intelligent understanding of the business world.
Uh-huh, sure.
I bet you even gave him complimentary coffee.
I didn't charge him for his cappuccino if that's what you mean.
So your coffee shop didn't even make a profit on this guy.
And on top of that, you gave him a $4,000 check?
Hey, Dave, what's with you?
This guy was legit.
He was driving a Porsche for crying out loud.
Jenkins, did you even take the time to research and see if Ocean Tech was a real company?
I, uh, no, oh man, I was taken, wasn't I?
You were taken, but I won't be.
I'll see you later.
Let's learn the vocabulary from the dialogue.
David says he doesn't want to spend his hard-earned dollars.
This expression, hard-earned dollars, means money that required a lot of work to earn.
But Jenkins says, is the chance of a lifetime, Dave?
Light not, man.
The phrasal verb, lighten up, means don't be so serious.
But David says, Jenkins, you're nuts if you think I'm going to invest.
Nuts is a slang word for crazy.
David is calling his friend crazy.
You're nuts if you think I'm going to invest $4,000 into a stock that I know nothing about.
The word stock means a piece of ownership of a company and the total market, which is composed
of all the companies in the economy, is called the stock market.
David and Jenkins have been friends since childhood, so Jenkins says, you can trust me, man.
Would I lead you astray?
This phrase, lead you astray, means deceive you or take you in the wrong direction.
But David says, yes you would.
Remember the time you talked me into buying that 1967 convertible Volkswagen?
Talked me into.
This means convinced me.
If you talk someone into something, it means the other person didn't want to do it, but you
convinced them to change their mind.
David says that Volkswagen was a bad investment.
He says, that clunker cost me more in repairs than I care to remember.
The word clunker is a slang word for an old car that tends to break down very frequently.
Jenkins admits that he was wrong about that opportunity, but this one, he says, is different.
Ocean Tech is going to take the world by surprise.
This expression means surprise and amaze the world.
Ocean Tech is developing a new sonar technology.
The word sonar refers to technology for making scans underwater.
Jenkins says, Dave, if we invest now, will be millionaires.
Ocean Tech stocks are dirt cheap right now.
This expression, dirt cheap, means extremely inexpensive.
But David says he's never even heard of the company Ocean Tech, and he works for the Department
of Defense.
David says, if a deal involving the Navy was in the works, I would be aware of it.
In the works means in progress or being planned.
Jenkins says, dude, I'm your pal.
The word pal is an informal word for friend.
Jenkins continues, I'm offering you a chance of a lifetime and all you do is give me the
third degree.
This idiom, give me the third degree, means ask a lot of aggressive questions, interrogate
the person.
David explains that the reason he doesn't want to spend money is that he's saving up for
a down payment for a house.
A down payment is the initial payment for buying a house.
Usually when you buy a house, you don't pay all the money immediately.
You make an initial payment that's called the down payment and you pay the rest of it in
installments.
Then David says, I ain't about to gamble with my money.
This expression, I ain't, is a very informal way to say I'm not.
I ain't is not correct English, it's slang, so don't use it in professional situations.
I ain't about to gamble with my money.
The word gamble means take risks with money, which could result in losing it.
We also use the word gamble for the activity you do in casinos.
In casinos, you play games where you risk losing your money, so you are gambling with your money.
Jenkins claims that with this opportunity, you'll make a fortune.
The expression make a fortune means get a lot of money.
But David responds, nothing in life is that easy.
Sounds to me like this ocean tech company is a scam.
A scam is a fake opportunity which is designed to cheat people out of their money.
And David says, and man do you fall for scams.
Fall for is a phrasal verb in this context meaning believe in something that isn't true.
Then David makes a guess about how Jenkins heard about this opportunity.
He says, some smooth talking guy in a fancy suit came into your coffee shop.
Smooth talking describes someone who speaks well and can convince people, usually for
the purposes of deceiving people into believing things that aren't true.
Jenkins confirms that the guy who told him about this opportunity was a smooth talker.
And David also asks, and he used a lot of business lingo, right?
Lingo means specialized vocabulary in a certain area.
And David says, I bet you even gave him complimentary coffee.
The word complimentary means free.
David's saying that Jenkins gave this man a free coffee.
And Jenkins confirms that he did.
So David responds, so your coffee shop didn't even make a profit on this guy.
And on top of that, you gave him a $4,000 check.
On top of that means in addition.
Jenkins starts to protest, hey Dave what's with you?
This guy was legit.
Legit is short for legitimate, meaning real or trustworthy.
Jenkins adds, he was driving a Porsche for crying out loud.
A Porsche is a very fancy type of car.
And this expression, for crying out loud, is simply an informal expression that's used to
express annoyance.
Jenkins is annoyed with David's constant questions.
Finally, David asks if Jenkins even took the time to research and see if Ocean Tech was a real
company.
And Jenkins didn't do this.
He finally realizes, oh man, I was taken, wasn't I?
I was taken, is an informal way to say I was cheated or deceived.
David responds, you were taken, but I won't be.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
